list-item.p: CircRNAs drive tumor immune escape by regulating PD-L1 stability and reprogramming key immune cells within the TIME.
Therapeutically targeting or delivering circRNAs via nanocarriers can restore antitumor immunity and enhance treatment responses.
Advanced nanomedicine platforms enable precise, durable, and tumor-selective circRNA-based immunotherapy.

abstract.p: Circular RNAs (circRNAs), a class of covalently closed noncoding RNAs with remarkable stability and cell-type specificity, have emerged as critical regulators of cancer immunology. Increasing evidence reveals that circRNAs orchestrate tumor immune escape through multilayered mechanisms spanning post-transcriptional, post-translational, and metabolic levels, thereby reshaping the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). A central theme involves the maintenance of PD-L1 homeostasis: circRNAs modulate PD-L1 stability via m^6A/IGF2BP-dependent RNA–protein interactions, protect PD-L1 from ubiquitin-mediated degradation through deubiquitinases, or promote its phosphorylation to prevent proteasomal turnover. Beyond tumor-intrinsic regulation, circRNAs are packaged into exosomes or small extracellular vesicles and delivered to immune cells, where they induce CD8^+ T-cell dysfunction, foster regulatory T-cell expansion, or reprogram myeloid-derived suppressor cells and macrophages toward immunosuppressive phenotypes. These intercellular communications contribute to resistance against immune checkpoint inhibitors and conventional therapies. In parallel, circRNAs are increasingly recognized as both therapeutic targets and agents. Strategies that silence oncogenic circRNAs using nanoparticles restore drug sensitivity and reinvigorate antitumor immunity, while synthetic or in vitro–transcribed circRNAs encoding immunostimulatory factors such as IL-12 demonstrate potent capacity to remodel TIME. The integration of tumor-tailored lipid nanoparticles, biomimetic vesicles, and rational circRNA design underscores a new wave of precision immunotherapy. This review highlights the mechanistic diversity of circRNAs in immune evasion, their roles in therapeutic resistance, and the translational opportunities offered by nanomedicine-based delivery systems. By bridging basic immunology and therapeutic innovation, circRNAs hold promise as next-generation targets and tools in cancer immunotherapy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Cancer remains one of the foremost global health challenges, ranking as the second leading cause of death and accounting for nearly 20 million new cases and 10 million deaths each year according to the most recent GLOBOCAN statistics [1]. The global cancer burden continues to rise, driven by population aging, lifestyle transitions, and environmental risk factors, and survival disparities remain profound across regions and tumor types [2,3]. Although the past decade has witnessed remarkable progress with targeted therapies and immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), durable clinical benefit is restricted to a fraction of patients [[4], [5], [6], [7], [8]]. Most individuals either fail to respond initially or acquire resistance, highlighting the urgent need to identify novel regulatory pathways underlying immune escape [[9], [10], [11], [12], [13]]. The tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) is increasingly recognized as the decisive determinant of cancer progression and treatment response. Tumors deploy a repertoire of immune evasion strategies, including sustained PD-L1 upregulation, functional exhaustion of cytotoxic T lymphocytes, recruitment of immunosuppressive myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) and regulatory T cells (Tregs), and metabolic competition that deprives effector lymphocytes of nutrients [[14], [15], [16], [17], [18], [19]]. These adaptive mechanisms form a dynamic barrier to immunotherapy success and drive resistance across therapeutic modalities. Against this backdrop, noncoding RNAs have emerged as crucial regulators of the TIME [[20], [21], [22], [23]]. In particular, circular RNAs (circRNAs)—covalently closed, exonuclease-resistant transcripts characterized by stability, evolutionary conservation, and cell-type specificity—have gained increasing attention [[24], [25], [26], [27]]. Once considered transcriptional byproducts, circRNAs are now recognized as versatile regulators of gene expression, immune signaling, and metabolic adaptation, positioning them as potential key modulators at the interface of cancer biology and immunology [[28], [29], [30]].

Recent studies have revealed that circRNAs profoundly influence cancer immunology at multiple levels, acting as versatile regulators of tumor–immune interactions. At the adaptive immunity level, circRNAs modulate PD-L1 expression and stability through diverse mechanisms, including m^6A-dependent RNA–protein interactions, deubiquitination, and phosphorylation, thereby granting tumor cells robust protection against cytotoxic T-cell attack [17,31]. At the intercellular level, circRNAs are selectively packaged into exosomes or small extracellular vesicles and delivered to immune cells, where they orchestrate systemic immunosuppression by inducing CD8^+ T-cell exhaustion, promoting regulatory T-cell expansion, or reprogramming myeloid-derived suppressor cells and macrophages toward suppressive phenotypes [32]. Beyond immune escape, circRNAs also contribute to therapeutic resistance, linking oncogenic signaling with immunologic failure in the context of immune checkpoint blockade, endocrine therapy, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy [33]. Importantly, the translational landscape of circRNA research is rapidly evolving. Advances in nanotechnology and synthetic biology have enabled circRNAs to be targeted or repurposed as therapeutic tools [34,35]. On the one hand, antisense oligonucleotides or siRNAs delivered by biocompatible nanoparticles can silence oncogenic circRNAs, reversing PD-L1 stabilization, restoring drug sensitivity, and reinvigorating antitumor immunity [36]. On the other hand, engineered or in vitro–transcribed circRNAs encoding immunostimulatory cytokines such as IL-12 demonstrate remarkable potential to remodel the tumor immune microenvironment when encapsulated in tumor-tailored lipid nanoparticles or biomimetic vesicles [37]. Together, these advances position circRNAs not only as drivers of immune escape and resistance but also as promising therapeutic payloads in next-generation immuno-oncology. This review will summarize mechanistic insights into circRNA-mediated immune regulation, examine their role in therapy resistance, and highlight emerging opportunities where circRNA biology and nanomedicine converge to shape innovative strategies for cancer treatment.

In this review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the roles of circRNAs in cancer immunology, with a particular focus on three interconnected themes. First, we discuss how circRNAs regulate PD-L1 homeostasis and other immune checkpoints through multilayered mechanisms, including m^6A-dependent stabilization, deubiquitination, and phosphorylation. Second, we highlight the function of exosome-derived circRNAs in mediating intercellular communication, reprogramming immune cells, and driving resistance to immune checkpoint blockade. Third, we examine therapeutic opportunities, including nanoparticle-based delivery of circRNA inhibitors and synthetic circRNAs as immunostimulatory payloads. By integrating mechanistic insights with translational perspectives, we aim to establish circRNAs not only as drivers of tumor immune escape and therapeutic resistance but also as versatile tools in next-generation cancer immunotherapy.

sec.title: Functional classification of circRNAs
sec.p: Circular RNAs exert diverse biological functions through multiple molecular mechanisms, and these functional modalities collectively determine their regulatory impact on tumor immunity and therapeutic response. Broadly, circRNAs can be categorized into five major functional classes.

sec.title: Competing endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs)
sec.p: Many cytoplasmic circRNAs act as ceRNAs by sponging multiple microRNAs, thereby relieving miRNA-dependent repression of target mRNAs and reshaping oncogenic and immunologic signaling pathways. This mechanism is particularly prominent in the regulation of immune checkpoints [38]. For example, circRHBDD1 and circATAD2 sequester miRNAs that normally suppress PD-L1 transcription or translation, leading to sustained PD-L1 expression and facilitating tumor immune escape [39]. Similar ceRNA-mediated PD-L1 activation has been observed across diverse cancers, including lung, breast, gastric, and colorectal tumors, indicating that circRNA–miRNA–PD-L1 axes may represent a conserved immune evasion strategy. Beyond PD-L1 regulation, ceRNA activity enables circRNAs to modulate broader immunological processes such as cytokine production, T-cell exhaustion, macrophage polarization, and MDSC expansion. Certain circRNAs function as high-capacity miRNA reservoirs, binding dozens of miRNA molecules simultaneously due to multiple miRNA response elements (MREs) embedded within their circular structure. This multivalency provides circRNAs with stronger and more sustained regulatory potential compared to linear RNAs [40,41]. However, accumulating evidence reveals that ceRNA activity represents only one dimension of circRNA biology. High-throughput CLIP-seq and AGO2-RIP analyses indicate that only a minority of abundant circRNAs exhibit functionally meaningful miRNA binding, and many circRNAs lack sufficient MRE density to act as effective sponges. Moreover, the ceRNA effect requires favorable stoichiometric conditions—specifically, high circRNA abundance, co-localization with target miRNAs, and sufficient miRNA load, which are not universally present. These insights underscore a paradigm shift: while ceRNA activity contributes to immune escape, it accounts for only a subset of circRNA functions, and other mechanisms such as RBP scaffolding, post-transcriptional regulation, and nuclear transcriptional control may play equal or greater roles in shaping tumor immunity.

sec.title: RNA-binding protein (RBP) scaffolds and decoys
sec.p: CircRNAs frequently bind to RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), functioning not only as scaffolding platforms that facilitate protein–protein interactions but also as molecular decoys that sequester RBPs away from their canonical targets. This RBP-centered regulation represents one of the most versatile and powerful modes of circRNA activity, given their covalently closed structure, extended half-life, and high local concentration within specific subcellular compartments [42,43]. A growing number of circRNAs have been shown to modulate immune escape through RBP scaffolding. For example, circIGF2BP3 enhances the interaction between OTUB1 and PD-L1, promoting deubiquitination and stabilization of PD-L1 on the tumor cell surface [44]. Conversely, circNDUFB2 forms a ternary complex with TRIM25 and IGF2BPs, facilitating TRIM25-mediated K63-linked ubiquitination and degradation of IGF2BP proteins, thereby simultaneously suppressing oncogenic RNA stabilization and activating RIG-I–dependent innate immune responses [29]. Another representative example is circ_0067842, which enhances the binding of HuR to CMTM6, stabilizing PD-L1 and strengthening immune evasion in breast cancer [45]. These findings reveal that circRNAs can tune immune checkpoint signaling by dictating the composition and activity of RBP complexes. Beyond checkpoint regulation, circRNAs govern multiple immunologically relevant RBPs involved in cytokine transcription, antigen presentation, and T-cell exhaustion. Nuclear circRNAs such as circPHLPP2 cooperate with ILF3 to enhance IL-36γ transcription, shaping an inflammatory yet immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment [46]. Similarly, circRNAs have been reported to modulate RBPs like YBX1, LIN28A, or HNRNPL, all of which influence immune pathways ranging from interferon signaling to alternative splicing of immune regulators. As high-affinity RBP hubs, circRNAs can function as molecular “organizers,” coordinating the assembly, localization, and activity of regulatory protein complexes to fine-tune post-transcriptional gene expression. Collectively, these observations demonstrate that circRNA–RBP interactions constitute a central regulatory axis in tumor immunity. By rewiring RBP availability and function, circRNAs exert broad control over mRNA stabilization, translation, ubiquitination, and innate immune activation, underscoring their importance as upstream modulators of immune escape and therapeutic resistance.

sec.title: Template for protein translation
sec.p: Although circRNAs were historically classified as noncoding molecules, accumulating evidence has revealed that a subset of circRNAs possesses translational potential, generating functional peptides through internal ribosome entry sites (IRESs), m⁶A-dependent cap-independent initiation, or direct recruitment of ribosomal subunits. These translation-competent circRNAs have been identified across multiple cancer types and display diverse biological activities relevant to tumor progression, immune regulation, and therapy resistance. Several endogenous circRNA-encoded peptides have been functionally characterized. CircZNF609 encodes a peptide that modulates myogenesis and cellular stress responses, while circFBXW7 produces a tumor-suppressive peptide (FBXW7–185aa) that antagonizes c-Myc stability in glioma [47]. In hepatocellular carcinoma, circβ-catenin generates a β-catenin isoform that augments Wnt signaling, enhancing proliferation and resistance to immune-mediated cytotoxicity [48]. Importantly, some circRNA-derived peptides influence immune processes directly; for instance, circMAPK14 encodes a peptide that competes with MAPK14 for MKK6 binding, attenuating p38 signaling and shaping inflammatory pathways within the tumor microenvironment [49]. Beyond natural circRNAs, synthetic circRNAs engineered for translation have opened a new avenue in cancer immunotherapy. In preclinical models, circRNAs encoding immunostimulatory cytokines—such as IL-12, IL-15 superagonists, and IFN-β—exhibit prolonged and higher-fidelity protein expression compared with linear mRNAs, owing to their improved resistance to exonuclease degradation and reduced innate immune activation. Of particular relevance, tumor-targeted delivery of IL-12–encoding circRNAs via lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) has demonstrated potent antitumor immunity, enhancing NK-cell activation, promoting intratumoral CD8⁺ T-cell expansion, and overcoming resistance to immune checkpoint blockade [37]. Moreover, rational sequence engineering permits fine-tuning of immunogenicity; incorporation of m⁶A motifs or modified nucleotides enables the generation of either immune-silent or immune-activating circRNAs depending on therapeutic needs.

sec.title: Biogenesis regulation of circRNAs and its immunological implications
sec.p: CircRNA biogenesis is tightly controlled by RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), splicing factors, intronic complementarity, and exon selection, forming a regulatory layer that ultimately shapes circRNA-mediated immune modulation. Key splicing regulators such as QKI, ESRP1/2, FUS, HNRNPL, and DHX9 orchestrate exon circularization by promoting or suppressing back-splicing, thereby determining circRNA abundance in a cell type–specific manner [40,50]. Notably, several of these factors are dynamically regulated in cancer and are strongly influenced by inflammatory cues, oncogenic signaling, or hypoxia—conditions that also remodel the TIME [51,52]. Mechanistically, QKI is known to promote circRNA formation through QKI-binding motifs flanking circularized exons, and its upregulation in inflamed or hypoxic tumors can selectively enhance the production of immune-related circRNAs. Conversely, DHX9 suppresses circRNA formation by destabilizing intronic complementary sequences, and its downregulation in certain cancers leads to a global increase in circRNAs that promote immune evasion [53]. ESRP1/2, classical epithelial splicing factors, have been shown to regulate circRNA biogenesis in epithelial-type cancers such as breast and gastrointestinal cancers, and it is plausible that some of these circRNAs may influence PD-L1 stability or immune cell phenotypes, although direct evidence is still emerging [54]. These findings indicate that splicing factor dysregulation is an upstream driver of oncogenic circRNA landscapes, providing a mechanistic link between transcriptional stress, metabolic rewiring, and immunosuppressive circRNA profiles. Importantly, splicing-regulated circRNA biogenesis intersects with immune intervention strategies. In tumors where ESRP or QKI are aberrantly activated, inhibiting upstream splicing networks may reduce the generation of immunosuppressive circRNAs and enhance the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade. Conversely, leveraging splicing factor–guided back-splicing rules may improve the design of synthetic or therapeutic circRNAs with optimized expression and immunomodulatory properties. Together, these insights highlight circRNA biogenesis as a previously underappreciated axis of immune regulation and a potential therapeutic entry point within the tumor–immune interface.

sec.title: Mechanistic landscape: how circRNAs rewire tumor immunity
PD-L1 homeostasis and T-cell suppression
sec.p:
PD-L1 expression and stability are central determinants of tumor immune evasion, as they directly control the inhibitory PD-1 signaling that dampens cytotoxic T-cell activity [[55], [56], [57], [58]]. CircRNAs have emerged as potent upstream regulators of PD-L1 homeostasis, acting through multiple molecular layers to provide tumors with sustained protection from immune surveillance. Importantly, comparative analyses across cancer types reveal that some of these regulatory patterns are highly conserved, whereas others display tumor-specific characteristics, reflecting the distinct immune-microenvironmental pressures faced by different malignancies. At the RNA level, several circRNAs—including circATAD2 in breast cancer and circRHBDD1 in gastric cancer—converge on the m⁶A–IGF2BP axis to stabilize PD-L1 mRNA, suggesting that IGF2BP-mediated protection represents a shared regulatory paradigm across cancers [32,39]. Similarly, m^6A-modified circIGF2BP3 increases the abundance of OTUB1, a deubiquitinase that shields PD-L1 from proteasomal degradation in NSCLC [44]. At the protein level, circ_0136666 promotes PD-L1 phosphorylation via the miR-375/PRKDC axis in gastric cancer, a post-translational modification that further enhances PD-L1 stability [17]. Conversely, in breast cancer, circ_0067842 reinforces membrane retention of PD-L1 through HuR/CMTM6 interactions, ensuring prolonged PD-1 engagement by infiltrating T cells [45]. These examples illustrate mechanistic divergence among tumor types, with distinct circRNA signatures tailoring PD-L1 regulation to the metabolic, inflammatory, or stromal features of each cancer. Collectively, these findings position circRNAs as “multi-tier guardians” of PD-L1—acting from mRNA stabilization to post-translational modification and membrane localization. Notably, the coexistence of conserved (e.g., IGF2BP-dependent mRNA protection) and cancer-specific mechanisms (e.g., PRKDC-mediated PD-L1 phosphorylation in gastric cancer) highlights the complexity of circRNA-based immune evasion across malignancies. This mechanistic diversity carries important translational implications: tumors enriched in circRNAs converging on PD-L1 regulation may exhibit intrinsic resistance to immune checkpoint blockade. As illustrated in Fig. 1, circRNAs coordinate complementary regulatory mechanisms to construct a robust barrier against T-cell immunity. Future studies leveraging patient-derived cohorts, CLIP-seq–verified RBP binding data, and lineage-specific in vivo models will be essential to determine whether circRNA-mediated PD-L1 stabilization constitutes a universal hallmark of immune escape or a context-dependent phenomenon shaped by individual tumor ecosystems.Fig. 1
CircRNA-mediated multi-layer regulation of PD-L1 stability and T-cell inhibition.Fig 1

sec.title: Exosomal circRNAs and systemic immune suppression
sec.p:
Exosomes and small extracellular vesicles (sEVs) are critical mediators of intercellular communication, enabling tumor cells to extend immunoregulatory signals beyond the local microenvironment [[59], [60], [61], [62], [63]]. Importantly, recent quantitative profiling studies—including circRNA-seq of patient-derived plasma exosomes—demonstrate that circRNAs are often preferentially enriched in sEVs compared with their linear isoforms, with some circRNAs showing 10–50-fold higher vesicular abundance. Such selective packaging not only enhances stability in circulation but also endows circRNAs with the capacity to exert systemic immunomodulatory effects. Emerging evidence from multiple experimental models (e.g., tumor-conditioned media, immune co-culture assays, patient-derived exosomes, and in vivo xenograft models) indicates that exosomal circRNAs act as potent suppressors of both adaptive and innate immunity. In NSCLC, exosomal circUSP7 is present at significantly higher levels in anti–PD-1–refractory patient plasma and functions by sponging miR-934 to increase SHP2 expression, thereby robustly impairing CD8⁺ T-cell activation [18]. In gastric cancer, sEVs enriched in circ_0001947 induce a dose-dependent exhaustion phenotype in CD8⁺ T cells—characterized by elevated PD-1, TIM-3, and LAG-3 expression—which reduces cytotoxicity and compromises anti–PD-1 responsiveness [64]. Meanwhile, bladder cancer–derived exosomal circ_0013936 specifically targets PMN-MDSCs, increasing fatty acid uptake via FATP2 and suppressing RIPK3-mediated necroptosis, ultimately enhancing their suppressive activity in both in vitro differentiation assays and in vivo tumor-bearing mouse models [19]. These findings reveal that the immunosuppressive potency of exosomal circRNAs differs across immune cell types, with CD8⁺ T cells exhibiting functional impairment and exhaustion, Tregs showing expansion in multiple cohorts, PMN- and M-MDSCs undergoing metabolic reprogramming and enhanced survival, and macrophages shifting toward M2-like polarization as reported in several studies. Such cell type–specific heterogeneity underscores the capacity of exosomal circRNAs to orchestrate systemic immune suppression by simultaneously disrupting multiple arms of both adaptive and innate immunity (Fig. 2). Beyond mechanistic insights, clinical evidence further demonstrates that circulating exosomal circRNAs—such as circUSP7, circHIPK3, circFARSA, and circ0000190—are strongly associated with immune checkpoint inhibitor resistance, immune-excluded tumor phenotypes, and patient outcomes, highlighting their potential as minimally invasive biomarkers for monitoring immune status. Therapeutically, these observations suggest that targeting the biogenesis, selective sorting, release, or uptake of immunosuppressive circRNA-enriched vesicles may offer a promising strategy for restoring antitumor immunity, whereas engineered exosomes delivering therapeutic circRNAs or circRNA inhibitors could represent a next-generation immunomodulatory platform. Future studies integrating quantitative vesicleomics, standardized exosome isolation workflows, and comparative analyses across patient-derived samples will be crucial for precisely delineating the circRNA species that drive systemic immune suppression and for advancing their clinical translation.Fig. 2
Exosomal circRNAs mediate systemic immune suppression by targeting T cells and MDSCs.Fig 2

sec.title: Innate immunity, cytokines, and nuclear regulation
sec.p:
Innate immune signaling and cytokine expression are critical determinants of the tumor immune microenvironment, bridging early pathogen-like recognition with downstream adaptive immunity [[65], [66], [67]]. CircRNAs, once regarded as cytoplasmic miRNA sponges, are now recognized as versatile regulators that also act at the level of protein–RNA interactions and nuclear transcriptional control. A striking example is circNDUFB2, which promotes TRIM25-mediated ubiquitination and degradation of oncogenic IGF2BPs while concurrently activating RIG-I–dependent type I interferon responses in NSCLC [29]. This dual mechanism not only destabilizes immune checkpoint regulators but also enhances antiviral-like signaling, thereby exerting tumor-suppressive and immunostimulatory effects. In contrast, nuclear-localized circPHLPP2 exemplifies the oncogenic facet of circRNAs. By binding to the RNA-binding protein ILF3, circPHLPP2 upregulates IL-36γ transcription in colorectal cancer, creating a pro-inflammatory but paradoxically immunosuppressive milieu that fosters tumor progression and confers resistance to PD-1 blockade [46]. CircRNAs exert context-dependent dual effects on innate immune signaling and cytokine networks(Fig. 3). These contrasting findings underscore the dualistic roles of circRNAs in innate immunity and cytokine regulation: some amplify anti-tumor immune pathways, while others remodel cytokine networks to reinforce immune escape. Translationally, these results highlight the potential of circRNAs both as therapeutic adjuvants to boost innate sensing and as actionable targets to disrupt cytokine-driven resistance. Future research should clarify the determinants that govern whether a circRNA exerts pro-immune or immunosuppressive functions, and establish systematic methods to capture their nuclear versus cytoplasmic roles in cancer immunology.Fig. 3
Dual roles of circRNAs in innate immunity, cytokine regulation, and tumor immune response.Fig 3

sec.title: Metabolic–Immune coupling
sec.p:
Metabolic rewiring is a hallmark of cancer and a critical determinant of immune evasion, as tumors compete with infiltrating lymphocytes for energy substrates and exploit metabolic byproducts to suppress immune function [[68], [69], [70], [71]]. CircRNAs have emerged as important regulators at this intersection, directly linking oncogenic metabolism with immune escape. While metabolic alterations such as enhanced glycolysis, fatty acid uptake, and dysregulated amino acid utilization have long been implicated in shaping the TIME, recent findings reveal that circRNAs operate as upstream regulators that coordinate these bioenergetic shifts with immunosuppressive programs [72,73]. Emerging evidence positions circRNAs not merely as passive byproducts of RNA splicing but as active metabolic orchestrators that integrate oncogenic metabolism with immune dysfunction. At the level of glucose metabolism, circRNAs reinforce the Warburg effect to promote immune escape. In NSCLC, circRUNX1 enhances the Warburg effect by regulating the miR-145/HK2 axis, thereby fueling glycolysis-driven tumor growth while simultaneously limiting effector T-cell responses [74]. Similarly, in breast cancer, circ_002144 enhances glycolytic flux through the miR-326/PKM pathway, aggravating glucose deprivation within the TIME and weakening effector lymphocyte function [75]. Beyond glucose utilization, circRNAs also influence lactate accumulation—an immunosuppressive metabolite known to inhibit dendritic cell maturation, drive M2-like macrophage polarization, and promote Treg expansion. Although direct circRNA–lactate regulatory axes remain underexplored, early multi-omics datasets suggest that circRNAs may modulate key lactate transporters (e.g., MCT1/4) and LDHA, providing a rationale for future investigation. Lipid metabolic rewiring further expands the immunosuppressive impact of circRNAs. In bladder cancer, circZNF609 stabilizes CD36 via IGF2BP2, enhancing fatty acid uptake—a process that not only fuels tumor growth but also intensifies metabolic competition with CD8⁺ T cells, thereby diminishing responsiveness to immune checkpoint inhibitors [76]. As illustrated in Fig. 4, circRNAs function as critical metabolic checkpoints that couple tumor growth with immune evasion. Together, these findings highlight circRNAs as critical metabolic checkpoints that integrate bioenergetic programming with immune modulation. By simultaneously sustaining tumor growth and restricting nutrient availability to immune cells, circRNA-mediated metabolic rewiring creates a double burden on antitumor immunity. This dual role provides a compelling rationale for therapeutic interventions: combining circRNA-targeted strategies with metabolic inhibitors (e.g., glycolysis blockers or CD36 antagonists) could relieve immunometabolic stress and improve the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade.Fig. 4
CircRNA-mediated metabolic–immune coupling drives tumor immune evasion.Fig 4

Looking ahead, future studies should adopt multi-omics approaches—integrating circRNA profiling with metabolomics, single-cell transcriptomics, and spatial reconstruction of metabolic heterogeneity—to map the circRNA–metabolism–immunity network with greater granularity. Additional pathways, including oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial biogenesis, and lactate signaling, may also be governed by circRNA-driven regulation. Deciphering these mechanisms will not only enhance biological understanding but also unlock new therapeutic opportunities to reprogram tumor metabolism and restore antitumor immune competence.

sec.title: Other immune pathways and tumor stemness
sec.p: Beyond PD-L1 regulation and metabolic control, circRNAs also influence broader oncogenic pathways that intersect with immune evasion. A notable example is circFAT1, which activates STAT3 signaling, thereby enhancing cancer stemness and simultaneously suppressing immune surveillance. Since STAT3 serves as a central hub for maintaining tumor-initiating cell phenotypes while promoting an immunosuppressive cytokine milieu, circRNA-mediated STAT3 activation highlights a direct link between stemness and immune escape [77]. This suggests that circRNAs may function as upstream regulators coupling tumor plasticity with immune resistance. Although current mechanistic evidence is limited compared to PD-L1-focused studies, emerging data indicate that circRNAs may modulate additional immune-relevant pathways such as Wnt/β-catenin, Notch, or TGF-β signaling, all of which are closely tied to epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and stem-like properties [[78], [79], [80], [81]]. By reinforcing stemness and EMT programs, circRNAs may indirectly suppress antigen presentation, reduce T-cell infiltration, and promote resistance to immunotherapy. This expanding perspective broadens the scope of circRNA-mediated immune regulation and underscores the need for future research to systematically chart how circRNAs orchestrate the convergence of stemness pathways and immune evasion. Such studies could reveal circRNAs as critical “master regulators” of tumor adaptability and highlight new opportunities for therapeutic intervention at the interface of plasticity and immunology.

sec.title: Resistance to immune checkpoint blockade
sec.p:
Despite transforming the oncology landscape, ICIs provide durable benefit only to a minority of patients, with both primary and acquired resistance posing major barriers to clinical efficacy[[82], [83], [84], [85], [86]]. CircRNAs are increasingly recognized as critical contributors to these resistance mechanisms by reinforcing PD-L1 expression and shaping immunosuppressive circuits. Several circRNAs safeguard PD-L1 against degradation: circIGF2BP3 promotes deubiquitination through OTUB1, while circ_0136666 induces PRKDC-mediated phosphorylation to prevent proteasomal turnover, both of which attenuate CD8^+ T-cell cytotoxicity [32,87]. At the intercellular level, exosomal circUSP7 impairs CD8^+ T-cell function via the miR-934/SHP2 axis, and sEV-derived circ_0001947 drives CD8^+ T-cell exhaustion in gastric cancer, collectively exacerbating immune dysfunction and resistance to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade [18,64]. Nuclear circPHLPP2 further broadens this regulatory spectrum by activating IL-36γ transcription, generating an inflammatory yet immunosuppressive cytokine milieu that undermines ICI responsiveness [46]. As shown in Fig. 5, circRNAs act at multiple levels to promote resistance against PD-1/PD-L1 immune checkpoint blockade. These diverse mechanisms underscore circRNAs as central players in both primary and acquired resistance to immunotherapy. Their ability to stabilize PD-L1, reprogram immune effector cells, and reshape cytokine networks illustrates a multi-layered resistance architecture that extends beyond canonical oncogenic signaling. Translationally, circRNAs hold promise as predictive biomarkers for stratifying patients likely to experience ICI resistance, especially when detected in circulating exosomes. Moreover, therapeutic targeting of oncogenic circRNAs—either by antisense oligonucleotides or nanoparticle-mediated delivery—could synergize with checkpoint blockade to overcome resistance. Future studies should prioritize integrating circRNA profiling into clinical trial frameworks to determine whether their inhibition can restore durable immunotherapy responses.Fig. 5
CircRNA-mediated mechanisms of resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs).Fig 5

sec.title: Resistance to endocrine therapy, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy
sec.p:
Resistance to conventional therapies such as endocrine therapy, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy remains a persistent challenge in oncology, and growing evidence implicates circRNAs as key mediators of these processes through both tumor-intrinsic and immunologic mechanisms [88]. In breast cancer, circTNK2 contributes to tamoxifen resistance, but nanoparticle-mediated silencing of circTNK2 combined with delivery of a CXCL10 plasmid restores drug sensitivity while simultaneously enhancing NK cell infiltration [89]. This finding underscores that circRNA targeting can reverse endocrine resistance not only by modulating tumor signaling but also by reactivating antitumor immunity. In hepatocellular carcinoma, exosomal circTMEM56 augments the STING pathway through the miR-136–5p axis, thereby improving the efficacy of radiotherapy by stimulating innate immune responses and enhancing immunogenic cell death [90]. Similarly, in lung cancer, circ-METTL15 upregulates PD-L1 expression via the miR-1299/PD-L1 axis, linking chemoresistance with immune evasion and demonstrating how circRNAs couple therapy resistance with suppression of T-cell activity [91]. CircRNAs exert dual functions in mediating resistance to endocrine therapy, chemotherapy, and radiotherapy, while simultaneously modulating immune responses(Fig. 6). Collectively, these studies reveal that circRNAs act as dual regulators of therapeutic resistance by reinforcing oncogenic pathways while simultaneously reshaping the tumor immune microenvironment. This dual role highlights an important translational insight: overcoming resistance may require combination strategies that simultaneously silence oncogenic circRNAs and restore immune function, for example by pairing circRNA-targeted nanoparticles with checkpoint inhibitors or immune adjuvants. Moving forward, systematic mapping of circRNA signatures associated with therapy resistance and integrating them into biomarker-guided clinical trial designs will be essential to identify patient subsets that could benefit most from such dual targeting approaches.Fig. 6
CircRNA-mediated mechanisms of endocrine, chemo-, and radio-resistance with immunological implications.Fig 6

sec.title: Ferroptosis and immunotherapy synergy
sec.p:
Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by lipid peroxidation, has recently emerged as a critical determinant of tumor immunity [92]. Unlike apoptosis, ferroptosis releases damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) and lipid metabolites that enhance dendritic cell activation and T-cell priming, thereby boosting antitumor immune responses [93]. Resistance to ferroptosis not only supports tumor survival under oxidative stress but also diminishes the immunogenicity of dying cancer cells, reducing the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade. CircRNAs are now being implicated as upstream regulators of ferroptosis, linking metabolic and redox pathways to immune escape. In pancreatic cancer, cTRIP12 has been identified as a circRNA that promotes ferroptosis resistance, and its inhibition enhances susceptibility to lipid peroxidation while simultaneously sensitizing tumors to PD-1/PD-L1 blockade [94]. CircRNAs are emerging regulators of ferroptosis with profound immunological consequences(Fig. 7). This highlights a critical intersection between circRNA-mediated regulation of cell death and responsiveness to immunotherapy. Although current evidence remains limited to preclinical models, the therapeutic implications are substantial. Targeting circRNAs that inhibit ferroptosis could lower the threshold for immune-mediated tumor clearance, especially when combined with ferroptosis inducers or checkpoint inhibitors. Future research should systematically chart circRNA–ferroptosis networks across cancer types, evaluate their impact on immune cell function, and determine whether circRNA signatures can stratify patients for combined ferroptosis–immunotherapy regimens.Fig. 7
CircRNA-mediated regulation of ferroptosis and its impact on immunotherapy response.Fig 7

sec.title: Therapeutic toolkits: from anti-oncogenic circRNAs to therapeutic circRNAs
Targeting oncogenic circRNAs with delivery platforms
sec.p:
Silencing oncogenic circRNAs represents a promising therapeutic avenue to reverse immune escape and overcome resistance, but efficient and tumor-selective delivery remains a major challenge [[95], [96], [97], [98]]. Owing to their covalently closed structure, circRNAs exhibit high stability and are often inaccessible to conventional RNAi approaches, necessitating innovative delivery platforms. Nanoparticle-based systems provide an attractive solution by improving stability, biodistribution, and cellular uptake of circRNA-targeting molecules such as antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) or siRNAs. For example, PLGA/PEG nanoparticles loaded with circRHBDD1 inhibitors reduce PD-L1 stabilization in gastric cancer, thereby restoring T-cell immunity and sensitizing tumors to checkpoint blockade [39]. Similarly, ZIF-8 metal–organic framework nanoparticles have been engineered to co-deliver circTNK2 ASOs and a CXCL10 plasmid in breast cancer, simultaneously restoring tamoxifen sensitivity and recruiting NK cells, illustrating how dual payloads can target both oncogenic signaling and immune activation [89]. Beyond synthetic polymers and MOFs, biomimetic strategies are gaining momentum. Neutrophil membrane–coated nanoparticles, for instance, exploit immune cell homing properties to achieve precise delivery of circRNA inhibitors into inflamed or metastatic niches, as demonstrated in HER2-positive breast cancer brain metastases [99]. Such approaches not only improve targeting but also minimize systemic toxicity, a key consideration for clinical translation. Nanotechnology-based delivery systems offer versatile strategies to therapeutically target oncogenic circRNAs and overcome therapy resistance(Fig. 8). Together, these delivery strategies demonstrate that circRNAs can be pharmacologically suppressed with high specificity and therapeutic impact. Translationally, they provide a rationale for rational combinations with immune checkpoint inhibitors or chemotherapies, offering a pathway to overcome both immune escape and drug resistance. Future work should focus on optimizing nanoparticle formulations for clinical-grade manufacturing, ensuring reproducibility, and integrating circRNA-targeted nanomedicines into biomarker-driven patient stratification frameworks.Fig. 8
Nanoparticle-based delivery strategies targeting oncogenic circRNAs to restore antitumor immunity and overcome therapeutic resistance.Fig 8

sec.title: Synthetic circRNAs as therapeutic payloads
sec.p: Beyond functioning as therapeutic targets, circRNAs can also be rationally engineered as synthetic RNA drugs, taking advantage of their inherent stability, resistance to exonuclease degradation, and translational potential [100,101]. Unlike linear mRNAs, synthetic circRNAs exhibit prolonged half-life and sustained protein expression, making them attractive for durable immunomodulation in the tumor immune microenvironment. A prominent example is the delivery of IL-12 circRNAs via tumor-tailored ionizable LNPs in lung cancer, which achieved robust remodeling of the TIME, promoted CD8^+ T-cell expansion, and generated durable antitumor immunity [37]. This approach demonstrates the potential of circRNAs as immunostimulatory payloads capable of amplifying checkpoint blockade efficacy or even functioning as standalone immunotherapies. Another emerging strategy involves designing circRNAs to act as cytotoxic agents independent of protein translation [102]. An in vitro–transcribed circRNA engineered to bind cardiolipin on the mitochondrial inner membrane selectively ablated EIF4G2^+/PTBP1^+ adenocarcinoma cells across multiple cancer types, offering a novel RNA-based approach to directly eliminate malignant cells [103]. Together, these studies highlight the versatility of circRNA-based therapeutics, spanning immune reactivation and direct tumoricidal effects. From a translational perspective, rational design of synthetic circRNAs will require careful attention to sequence optimization, immunogenicity, and delivery selectivity. Moreover, combining engineered circRNAs with immune checkpoint inhibitors or metabolic modulators could provide synergistic therapeutic benefit. While circRNA-targeted therapeutics combined with ICIs hold substantial promise, several important clinical considerations remain underexplored. First, immune-related adverse events (irAEs) may be amplified when circRNA-based modulation enhances effector T-cell activation or cytokine release, raising the possibility of autoimmune manifestations similar to, or even exceeding, those associated with ICIs alone. Second, the long-term sustainability of circRNA therapeutics is uncertain, as synthetic circRNAs often exhibit extended intracellular persistence, which may lead to prolonged immune stimulation or delayed toxicity. Third, emerging resistance mechanisms must be considered: tumors may adapt by altering circRNA biogenesis pathways, activating compensatory immunosuppressive circuits (e.g., alternative immune checkpoints), or remodeling lipid and RNA-binding protein networks to evade nanocarrier-mediated delivery. These factors underscore the need for rigorous preclinical assessment of circRNA pharmacodynamics, longitudinal immune profiling, and rational design of combination strategies to balance therapeutic potency with safety. Incorporating these dimensions will be essential for translating circRNA-based immunotherapies into durable and clinically viable interventions. These findings position circRNAs as a new frontier in RNA medicine, bridging immunotherapy and precision oncology.

sec.title: Safety, pharmacokinetics, and CMC considerations
sec.p: The therapeutic development of circRNAs demands rigorous evaluation of safety, pharmacokinetics, and manufacturability before clinical translation. A primary concern is immunogenicity: synthetic or in vitro–transcribed circRNAs may inadvertently trigger innate immune sensors such as RIG-I or MDA5, particularly if dsRNA contaminants are present after transcription [[104], [105], [106]]. This can lead to uncontrolled cytokine release and toxicity resembling cytokine storm syndromes. Similarly, chemical modifications or nanoparticle carriers may introduce additional immunostimulatory effects, necessitating careful preclinical screening to distinguish therapeutic activity from off-target immune activation. Pharmacokinetic and biodistribution profiles pose further challenges. Lipid nanoparticles and polymeric carriers frequently accumulate in the liver and spleen, raising the risk of off-target effects and dose-limiting toxicity. For circRNA-based drugs, persistence and degradation pathways remain poorly characterized, complicating the prediction of therapeutic window and dosing schedules. Understanding how circRNA length, structure, and chemical modifications influence circulation half-life and clearance will be critical for optimizing clinical performance. From a manufacturing perspective, chemistry, manufacturing, and control (CMC) considerations are equally pressing. Scalable production of circRNAs requires robust in vitro transcription and efficient circularization strategies, coupled with stringent purification methods to eliminate linear RNA byproducts and dsRNA contaminants. Batch-to-batch consistency, stability during storage, and cost-effective scale-up will determine the feasibility of circRNA therapeutics in real-world clinical settings. Looking forward, future progress will depend on the development of tumor-selective formulations that enhance on-target delivery while minimizing systemic exposure. Strategies may include tumor-homing nanoparticles, biomimetic coatings, or conditional circRNA expression systems activated by tumor-specific cues. At the clinical level, standardized safety frameworks and pharmacovigilance protocols will be essential to monitor adverse events, particularly when circRNAs are combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors or metabolic modulators. Addressing these safety, PK, and CMC challenges is a prerequisite to unlocking the full therapeutic potential of circRNA-based interventions.

sec.title: Biomarkers, patient stratification, and clinical translation
sec.p: CircRNAs hold significant promise as next-generation biomarkers for cancer immunology, owing to their covalently closed structure, resistance to exonuclease degradation, and remarkable stability in body fluids [[107], [108], [109], [110], [111]]. These features make circRNAs particularly well-suited for non-invasive detection via liquid biopsy. Several exosomal circRNAs, such as circ_0072309 in gastric cancer, have been correlated with immune infiltration patterns and clinical outcomes, while circRNA–miRNA–mRNA networks identified in colorectal and oral squamous cell carcinoma have been linked to distinct immune signatures [112]. These findings underscore the value of circRNAs as stable, accessible, and disease-specific biomarkers that can complement or refine existing genomic and immunologic predictors such as tumor mutational burden (TMB) or PD-L1 immunohistochemistry. Patient stratification based on circRNA expression is emerging as a translationally relevant application. Tumors enriched in circRNAs that stabilize PD-L1 (e.g., circRHBDD1, circATAD2, circIGF2BP3) or promote lipid metabolic reprogramming (e.g., circZNF609) are likely to exhibit poor responsiveness to checkpoint blockade, providing a rationale for circRNA-targeted combination strategies [32,39,44]. Incorporating circRNA profiling into clinical trial design may enable biomarker-driven basket or umbrella trials, in which patient enrollment is guided by specific circRNA signatures rather than tumor histology alone. Moreover, liquid biopsy detection of exosomal circRNAs via advanced technologies such as digital droplet PCR (ddPCR), next-generation RNA sequencing, or nanopore platforms offers a practical route for real-time monitoring of therapy resistance and immune escape dynamic [[113], [114], [115], [116]]. s Despite these opportunities, significant challenges remain for clinical translation. Technical barriers include assay standardization, normalization across sequencing platforms, and the establishment of validated reference databases for circRNA signatures. Biological variability, such as tumor heterogeneity and exosomal circRNA sorting mechanisms, also complicates interpretation. Furthermore, early-phase clinical development of circRNA-based therapeutics must address regulatory requirements for safety, pharmacokinetics, and chemistry, manufacturing, and control (CMC) standards. Integration with artificial intelligence and multi-omics approaches—including transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics—could help decode circRNA-mediated immune regulation and improve predictive accuracy. With these considerations, circRNAs have the potential to evolve into both companion diagnostics and therapeutic agents, bridging mechanistic insights with precision immuno-oncology and improving patient selection for next-generation therapies.

sec.title: Reporting standards, reproducibility, and pitfalls
sec.p: The rapid expansion of circRNA research in cancer immunology has generated numerous discoveries, yet it has also exposed recurring challenges of reproducibility, methodological rigor, and translational reliability [[117], [118], [119]]. Reliable identification of circRNAs requires stringent validation beyond bioinformatic predictions. While RNA-seq has enabled global circRNA profiling, computational pipelines differ in sensitivity and specificity, often producing inconsistent or false-positive back-splice junction calls. Best practice involves integrating multiple algorithms, confirming BSJs by divergent primers and Sanger sequencing, and assessing RNase R resistance to rule out linear RNA artifacts [120]. Subcellular localization by fractionation or FISH should also be incorporated to contextualize functional relevance, since many circRNAs exert effects in specific compartments such as the cytoplasm or nucleus. Functional validation demands equally rigorous standards. Over-reliance on ectopic overexpression systems without parallel loss-of-function or rescue experiments risks misattributing phenotypes. For instance, establishing circRNA regulation of PD-L1 requires knockdown complemented by re-expression of circRNA constructs, combined with RNA–protein interaction assays (RIP/CLIP) to confirm binding to RBPs such as IGF2BPs [29,39]. Similarly, epitranscriptomic modifications like m^6A must be validated with orthogonal techniques including MeRIP-seq, site-specific mapping, and mutational analyses. The lack of methodological diversity has contributed to irreproducible findings, exemplified by the retraction of studies such as circ-CPA4, which underscores the importance of transparency and independent replication. Exosomal circRNA studies introduce further pitfalls [[121], [122], [123]]. Challenges include isolating pure vesicles free of cellular RNA contamination, quantifying circRNA abundance accurately, and demonstrating selective loading mechanisms. Many reports attribute immune effects to exosomal circRNAs without rigorous in vivo validation, increasing the risk of overinterpretation. Standardized methods for exosome isolation (e.g., ultracentrifugation vs. size-exclusion chromatography), normalization strategies, and characterization by minimal information for studies of extracellular vesicles (MISEV) guidelines are essential for meaningful cross-study comparisons. Finally, systemic biases also hinder progress. Publication bias toward positive results, insufficient reporting of negative findings, and limited cross-cohort validation reduce confidence in circRNA signatures as reliable biomarkers. In clinical contexts, reproducibility is further challenged by inter-patient heterogeneity, differences in sequencing depth, and variability in circRNA detection platforms. Moving forward, the field would benefit from consensus guidelines and reproducibility checklists covering circRNA detection, functional assays, exosome characterization, and integration with multi-omics datasets. Adoption of FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) data standards and cross-laboratory benchmarking efforts will be critical to bridge the reproducibility gap. Only through standardized and transparent practices can circRNAs transition from exploratory findings to robust biomarkers and therapeutic tools in cancer immuno-oncology.

sec.title: Outlook: opportunities and open questions
sec.p: CircRNAs represent a rapidly expanding frontier in cancer immunology, yet their biology and translational potential are only beginning to be understood [[124], [125], [126]]. On the fundamental level, there is an urgent need to establish comprehensive circRNA atlases across tumor types and immune contexts, integrating bulk RNA-seq with single-cell and spatial transcriptomic approaches. Such efforts would resolve cell type–specific circRNA expression within the TIME, identify circRNAs enriched in T cells, myeloid cells, or cancer stem–like niches, and clarify their roles in shaping immune infiltration and therapeutic response. Mechanistic questions also remain unanswered: How are circRNAs selectively packaged into exosomes? What governs their subcellular localization between the nucleus and cytoplasm? And how do circRNA–protein interactions integrate with epitranscriptomic modifications such as m^6A to influence immune signaling? Addressing these gaps will provide the mechanistic depth required for clinical translation. On the therapeutic front, circRNAs offer unprecedented opportunities as programmable RNA drugs. Advances in RNA engineering now enable the design of synthetic circRNAs encoding immunostimulatory cytokines (e.g., IL-12), chemokines, or logic-gated modules that activate only in tumor-specific contexts. Coupled with tumor-tailored lipid nanoparticles, biomimetic coatings, or hybrid delivery platforms, such synthetic circRNAs could overcome long-standing barriers of stability, biodistribution, and specificity. In parallel, oncogenic circRNAs that regulate PD-L1, metabolic checkpoints, or exosomal immune signaling remain attractive nodes for silencing via antisense oligonucleotides, RNAi, or CRISPR-based strategies [[127], [128], [129], [130]]. However, translation faces significant challenges: minimizing off-target immune activation and cytokine storm, managing biodistribution biases toward liver and spleen, and establishing scalable GMP-compliant manufacturing pipelines. Looking forward, rigorous clinical trial design will be essential. Biomarker-driven patient stratification, real-time monitoring of exosomal circRNAs, and integration of pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (PK/PD) and immune monitoring endpoints should be embedded into early-phase studies. Incorporating artificial intelligence and multi-omics integration may accelerate the discovery of predictive circRNA signatures and guide individualized therapeutic design. Ultimately, the synergy between circRNA biology, immunotherapy, and nanomedicine holds the promise to reshape precision oncology. Yet, success will hinge on a careful balance between innovation and reproducibility, ensuring that circRNA-based interventions are not only scientifically compelling but also clinically safe, scalable, and impactful for patients.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Cancer continues to impose a growing global health burden, with millions of new cases and deaths annually, underscoring the urgent need for innovative strategies to overcome immune escape and therapy resistance. In this context, circRNAs have emerged as versatile regulators of tumor immunity, operating across multiple mechanistic layers. They stabilize PD-L1 through m^6A-dependent recruitment of IGF2BPs, deubiquitination, and phosphorylation; reprogram immune cell populations via exosomal transfer; and rewire metabolic circuits that deprive effector lymphocytes of essential resources. Such multi-tiered regulation positions circRNAs as central nodes linking oncogenic signaling with immunosuppressive remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment. At the same time, circRNAs are increasingly recognized as both biomarkers and therapeutic tools. On the diagnostic front, their stability and detectability in blood and exosomes make them attractive for non-invasive monitoring of immune activity, resistance, and prognosis. On the therapeutic front, nanoparticle-mediated inhibition of oncogenic circRNAs has restored immune surveillance in preclinical models, while synthetic circRNAs encoding immunostimulatory cytokines or tumoricidal modules have shown proof-of-concept as RNA-based drugs. Together, these advances highlight the translational potential of circRNAs to complement or even reshape current immunotherapy paradigms. The field now stands at a critical juncture. While circRNAs offer unprecedented opportunities for biomarker discovery and next-generation RNA therapeutics, significant challenges remain in reproducibility, assay standardization, safety, biodistribution control, and GMP-compliant manufacturing. Future progress will require the integration of multi-omics profiling, advanced delivery systems, and biomarker-driven clinical trial design, combined with rigorous reproducibility standards and real-world validation. Ultimately, by bridging mechanistic insight with therapeutic innovation, circRNAs may redefine strategies for overcoming immune escape and resistance, bringing the promise of more durable, precise, and personalized immunotherapy closer to reality.
